claims.title: Per-capita emissions vs 2030 projection
claims.claim: Climate Action Authority (13 Nov 2025): emissions per capita have fallen 44% since 2005, well above the EU average of 34%, showing Malta is reducing emissions at household level and across the economy.
claims.counter: The same Commission report shows effort-sharing emissions 41% above 2005 in 2024 and projects +42% (existing measures) or +30% (planned measures) by 2030 against a -19% target: the largest gap in the EU in percentage points. Malta was over its yearly ESR limit by 22, 25 and 30 points in 2022-2024 (+43/+42/+41% vs +21/+16/+11%); the 2021 surplus carried forward brings the cumulative balance to 0.0 Mt in 2024, -2.1 Mt projected for 2030 before flexibilities. Total emissions fell 27% (EU 33%); population grew 41%, explaining about half the per-person fall. Among the EU-27 (2005-2024) Malta ranks 3rd on the per-person cut (-48.5%) but 20th on the total cut (-27.4%). Transport +49%, F-gases about six-fold. In the authority's favour: effort-sharing emissions per person are flat (2.50 t in 2005, 2.52 t in 2024; proxy: total minus power generation), and no compliance shortfall has arisen before the first check in 2027.

location.place: Auberge de Castille (Office of the Prime Minister), Valletta

claims.speaker: Climate Action Authority; Ministry for the Environment

subclaims.text: Emissions per capita have fallen 44% since 2005
subclaims.finding: Reproduced from Eurostat (−46% to 2023, −48% to 2024). Commission source.

subclaims.text: …well above the EU average of 34%
subclaims.finding: Reproduced (−34% to 2023). True per person (3rd of 27 to 2024); not in total tonnes (−27% vs −33%; 20th of 27).

subclaims.text: Emissions per unit of GDP down 81.6% vs EU 61.9%
subclaims.finding: Not recomputed (GDP series and price base not stated). Direction consistent with Commission data.

subclaims.text: Malta is reducing emissions at household level
subclaims.finding: In total, sectors linked to households rose: transport +49%, buildings +9 to +12%, air-conditioning gases up almost six-fold. Per person, the target sectors were flat (2.50 t to 2.52 t, our estimate), not falling. A per-person ratio of all emissions is not a household measure.

subclaims.text: Malta’s efforts are showing clear results
subclaims.finding: True for power generation. The same report shows Malta over its yearly limits since 2022 and projects the largest shortfall in the EU (in percentage points) against its binding 2030 target; the release mentions neither.

subclaims.text: Malta aims to reduce emissions by 40% by 2030
subclaims.finding: A stated aim, not a result. Scope (total or effort-sharing) not given. Same figure appears in the 2026 Labour manifesto (see CC-011).

claims.quote: Emissions per capita have fallen by 44% since 2005, well above the EU average of 34%.

claims.claim: Ministry for the Environment (19 Jan 2026): Malta continues to make strong progress in waste management; mixed waste down over 30% to 95.5 million kg; about 412 million kg diverted from landfill over five years; the Long-Term Waste Management Plan is working.
claims.counter: Municipal recycling rate 16.7% in 2024 (EU 48.1%; 2025 target 55%), second-lowest of the 20 states with 2024 data; 79% of treated municipal waste landfilled. The 412 million kg cannot be reconciled with Eurostat (271 kt recycled or recovered, 2020-24); the 141 million kg baseline has no year. In fairness, the rate rose 7.6 points 2019-2024 (4th-largest rise of 20 EU states) and packaging recycling rose from 30.8% to 43.4% in 2023. (ERA's 68% figure is explicitly for construction waste and is not part of this claim.)

claims.title: “92% excellent” bathing water
claims.claim: Malta also shows excellent records under the Bathing Water Directive: 92% of Maltese bathing waters are of excellent quality.
claims.counter: The EEA series shows a decline: 86 of 87 sites were excellent in 2016–2018 (98.9%), then 85, 84, 84, 82, 80, 80 and 77 (88.5%) in 2025, the lowest of the eleven seasons since 2015. Balluta Bay's two sites (B08, B09) were rated only sufficient in every season 2022–2025, with a sewage-related warning from late May to 12 August 2024 inside that run. claims.title: Within EU limits vs WHO guideline
claims.claim: Newsbook (18 Jul 2025), reporting Parliamentary Question 29696: measurements taken between 2020 and 2024 at ERA's five PM2.5 monitoring stations are well above the WHO guideline but well within the less stringent EU annual limits.
claims.counter: All 23 reported station-year values exceed the WHO annual PM2.5 guideline of 5 µg/m³ and are below the EU annual limit of 25 µg/m³ applicable in 2020-2024. The annex marks St Paul's Bay as n/a for 2020 and 2021. Fourteen of 23 values exceed the EU limit of 10 µg/m³ due by 2030; this future standard does not establish past non-compliance. EEA validated daily data independently cross-check 11 station-years; ten match the annex to 0.1 µg/m³. Attard 2024 differs (12.122 µg/m³ from the EEA valid-day mean versus 11.9 in the annex), though both remain below 25 µg/m³.

claims.quote: However, the measurements taken between 2020 and 2024 in the five monitoring stations operated by the Environment and Resources Authority – at Attard, Msida, St Paul's Bay, Żejtun and Għarb – are well within the considerably less stringent annual limits set by the EU for fine particulate matter (PM2.5).

claims.title: Flyovers and congestion
claims.claim: Infrastructure Malta says the Msida Creek flyover will reduce delays, emissions and noise, and that the Marsa Junction Project has reduced travel time and air pollution.
claims.counter: The Msida Creek flyover opened to traffic on 18 December 2025, and the wider project remains under construction until 2027. At the only public air monitor near it (EEA sampling point MT00011, about 410 m away), mean NO2 for January–September 2026 was 25.2 µg/m³, against 22.0 in 2025 and 19.2 in 2024 (2026 data not yet validated); urban background stations rose about 4% and St Paul's Bay fell 6%, so the expected improvement has not appeared in the measured data. The Marsa release does not link the surveys behind its percentage claims, and no EEA-reported air monitor has operated within 1.4 km of the Marsa junction since Kordin (Paola) closed at the end of 2016. No project-level before-and-after series was found for traffic or noise at either site.
claims.speaker: Infrastructure Malta
claims.quote: Msida has long been a traffic bottleneck, with congestion impacting air quality, noise levels, and overall accessibility. A cornerstone of the Msida Creek Project is the construction of a new flyover to replace the current traffic-light-controlled junction, a critical move to reduce delays, emissions, and noise pollution, making travel smoother and safer for all road users.

claims.title: More RO, less WSC groundwater
claims.claim: WSC reported that reverse osmosis supplied 70.7% of its potable-water production in 2025, while groundwater production fell to 11.5 million m³, its lowest annual total in a decade. In August 2026, WSC issued a tender for a new 30,000 m³/day reverse-osmosis plant at Għar Lapsi.
claims.counter: The latest published River Basin Management Plan classifies both Malta and Gozo Mean Sea Level aquifer systems in poor quantitative status and 14 groundwater bodies in poor chemical status. Malta's reporting of the same cycle to the EEA lists four bodies in poor quantitative status (adding Pwales Coastal and Marfa Coastal) and all 15 in poor chemical status. The plan reports nitrate above the 50 mg/L standard in 12 of 15 bodies, with three named exceptions; not every body fails for nitrate. WSC's potable-production figures cover its supply system, not national abstraction. Eurostat estimates national fresh groundwater abstraction at 38.46 million m³ in 2024 (57% agriculture, up 3.1 million m³ on 2023), so WSC's 2025 cut of 1.55 million m³ is about 4% of it; a published water balance (Sapiano 2020) puts available groundwater at about 37 million m³ a year. Tracer ages of 15-40 years (Malta) and up to 60 or more (Gozo) mean water-quality recovery would take years to decades to show (Stuart et al. 2010).
claims.speaker: Water Services Corporation
claims.quote: “70.7% of this amount coming from the four Reverse Osmosis plants”

claims.claim: Project Green reported more than 8,000 trees and more than 25,000 shrubs planted by government entities in 2024. Pledge 305 of the 2022 Labour manifesto commits to 100,000 trees being planted over the next five years; a February 2026 parliamentary answer reports around 60,000 trees and over 100,000 shrubs planted through the end of 2025.

claims.title: Ta' Qali gravel and grass
claims.claim: Public Works Ministry (Sept 2025): the sand and gravel laid on the Ta' Qali picnic area retains moisture, so 'the natural grass grows at a much faster rate well before the rainfall of the winter season'; park unit head Jason Micallef: grass would grow back with the winter rains. claims.counter: Sentinel-2 (v1.1, reflectance offset applied): the 2.8 ha gravel zone (Momentum measured ~2.2 ha) greened every winter before the gravel (winter median NDVI 0.53-0.67 in 2023-2025, close to the rest of the park at 0.65-0.68) and stayed bare in winter 2025-26 (0.15) while the rest of the park was at 0.68. Summers were already bare before the gravel (~0.15), as the park management said. Gravel still in place and area bare in the last clear image, 27 Sep 2026. Soil-compaction reviews support the choking mechanism; gravel-sand mulch is a known water-conservation technique.

claims.title: Permits keep property prices in check
claims.claim: Planning Authority CEO Johann Buttigieg (MaltaToday interview, 2 Mar 2025): continuing to issue permits helps keep property prices in check; without them Malta would face the same housing crises as other European countries. The interviewer cited about 91,000 dwellings approved over a decade.
claims.counter: Supported in direction by peer-reviewed research on supply constraints (Glaeser et al. 2005; Hilber and Vermeulen 2016; Saiz 2010); Anenberg and Kung (2020) find extra supply alone does little for rent burdens. Malta population +31% 2015-2025 (EU +2%; highest of 27, about 16 times the EU rate); real house prices +34% (EU +25%; Malta 2025 provisional), which ranks 16th of 27, below the median Member State (+41%); the EU aggregate is weighted towards Germany, France and Italy (49%). Rents (HICP actual rentals) +53% vs EU +21% (8th of 27); house prices +6.9% a year to 2026-Q2 (provisional) vs EU +4.7%. Housing-cost overburden rose from 1.1% (2015) to 2.9% (2022) while the EU's fell; Eurostat flags a break in Malta's series in 2023, after which it held at about 6% (6.0% in 2025; EU 7.7%). Overcrowding 4.7% vs EU 16.8%. 27.5% of dwellings not a main residence (Census 2021).

location.place: Planning Authority, St Francis Ravelin, Floriana

claims.speaker: Johann Buttigieg, Planning Authority CEO

subclaims.text: Price is a supply-and-demand issue; more permits help keep prices in check
subclaims.finding: Supported in direction by peer-reviewed studies [5–7]; effect size uncertain and possibly small for affordability [8].

subclaims.text: Stopping permits would drive prices up
subclaims.finding: Consistent with the same research; not tested for Malta directly.

subclaims.text: Without the permits Malta would face the same crises as other European countries
subclaims.finding: Counterfactual. Malta is below the EU on overcrowding and overburden today, and its real price rise ranks 16th of 27 despite the fastest population growth; but its prices outpaced the EU aggregate, rents rose 53% (EU 21%) and overburden is rising.

subclaims.text: 91,000 dwellings in a decade (interviewer)

claims.quote: Had we not issued these permits, Malta would face the same housing crises as other European countries. This is a supply-and-demand issue – continuing to issue permits helps keep property prices in check. Stopping them would drive prices up.

claims.claim: Planning Authority CEO Johann Buttigieg (Malta Independent, 7 Sep 2025): the PA once issued over 1,000 enforcement notices a year and now about 200, which he attributed to fewer illegalities; over 5,000 cases await direct action and 1,500 illegalities were removed by direct action in 30 years.

claims.title: Shore-to-ship: 90% less harbour pollution
claims.claim: Infrastructure Malta (Shore-to-Ship project page, 1 Dec 2023): the Grand Harbour shore-to-ship initiative promises to slash 90% of air pollution in the Grand Harbour. Repeated at the inauguration (10 Jul 2024, cost given as EUR 33 million): completion means a 90% reduction, with 17,000 families around the harbour benefiting from cleaner air.
claims.counter: Connection is voluntary until 1 Jan 2030 (Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Art. 6); Transport Malta: connecting 'remains the prerogative of the shipping line'. Transport Malta FOI records (via Amphora Media): 67 of 373 cruise berths (18%) plugged in from Jul 2024 to Jul 2025, 9% of berth time; 306 berths not plugged in; MSC World Europa made 35 of the 67 (35 of its 51 calls; all other ships 32 of 322, 10%); no stay of 2-4 days plugged in. MSC World Europa is LNG-powered (dual-fuel LNG / low-sulphur marine gasoil, MSC Cruises 2022), so when it runs on LNG the SOx and PM saving from plugging it in is smaller than the per-liner figures. Cruise calls rose from 357 (2024) to 385 (2025; calendar years, while uptake runs Jul-Jul). Infrastructure Malta's own 2020-2023 pages scope the 90% to the pollution cruise liners and Ro-Ro ships produce, with per-liner cuts on shore power of NO2 -93%, PM -92.6%, SO2 -99.6%, CO2 -39.6% (study not cited); the 2023 project page dropped that scope. Research context: hotelling is >90% of cruise CO2 in port (Mocerino et al. 2026); manoeuvring emissions remain (Gagic et al. 2022). Cost stated as EUR 33m (launch), 37m (phase 1) and 49.9m (whole project). No harbour air-quality study before and after.

claims.title: Land reclamation outside the Freeport

No site, size, cost, fill source, screening or call for the large-scale project found by 3 Oct 2026. Seabed study unpublished since 2019; budget lines EUR 500,000 (2023) -> 10,000 (2025). Three Natura 2000 designations within ~0.5 km of the new Terminal 2 land, two of them overlapping on the same cliffs (SAC MT0000024, SPA MT0000033); marine SPA MT0000111 (256 km2) ~0.4 km away. v1.2: EMODnet Seabed Habitats (Maltese map of 2016, gridded at about 230 m) maps Posidonia next to the new land (0.01 km, one grid cell) and 72 ha within 1 km; EMODnet DTM 2024 depth within 1 km mostly 5-30 m (median 18 m); mapped meadows at 11-35 m in the bay (median 26 m) and 21-32 m within 1 km (median 29 m). A bay-wide Sentinel-2 MNDWI check for other new land was not robust and is not used.

claims.title: 830,000 m2 of land lost in five years
claims.claim: Amphora Media (Green to Grey, 11-12 Sep 2026): nearly 830,000 square metres of nature and cropland were built up in Malta between 2018 and 2023 (headline: 'over 830,000'), 0.26% of land; in nearly 95% of the take-up, farmland rather than natural area was affected.
claims.counter: v1.2: Amphora's published polygons (397) cover 828,429 m2, so 'nearly 830,000' is reproduced (the headline's 'over' is not). Spatial cross-check with Impact Observatory/Esri 10 m land cover (2017-2025): the model already maps 68% of Amphora's area as built-up in 2018 (61% in all of 2017-19), classes only 6-14% of it as newly built, and only 2-3% of its own new built-up land lies inside Amphora's polygons (5-7% within 20 m); its national net total ranges from -0.06 to 2.96 km2 depending on the rule and years. So the model measures different land and neither confirms nor rules out 0.83 km2 (v1.1 had read it as corroboration). 'Nearly 95%': cropland + grass = 96% (95.3-95.7%) of the area with a known 2018 class in Amphora's own data (our reading of the basis), counting Dynamic World 'grass' (which includes natural meadows) as farmland and leaving out the 37% of the area with no class; cropland alone is 22% of the whole. Two polygons (4,429 m2) were sea in 2018. Arithmetic (0.26%, 116 pitches, 1.94 km2 since 2006) checks out. EEA CORINE change maps: 20.6 ha (2006-12) and 93.7 ha (2012-18) of new artificial land, matching the 190,000 and 920,000 m2 quoted; changes under 5 ha are not mapped. Imagery spot-check (maintainer decision, 5 Oct 2026): 40 draws by systematic sampling proportional to area (seed 20261005, 39 polygons), checked by eye against Esri World Imagery Wayback (before Jul 2015-Aug 2016, 4 Sep 2018, 6 May 2023, Jun-Sep 2025): 72.5% of the sampled area confirmed open/green to grey (Wilson 95% CI 57-84%), 7.5% partial, 2.5% already grey, 0% still open, 17.5% unclear (15% being developed by Sep 2018); 55% (40-69%) confirmed and mostly grey by May 2023, so part of the figure is 2024-25 change. The imagery contradicts the model's 2018 built-up reading on these parcels. Land before: fields 59% (43-73%), 64% with orchards, the rest scrub, garrigue or rough grass, so 'nearly 95% farmland' is overstated. Verdict (maintainer decision, 5 Oct 2026): Not substantiated: about 456,000 m2 (330,000-574,000) was grey by May 2023 against 'nearly 830,000' for 2018-2023 (about 600,000 m2 by 2025), and about a third of the land was scrub or garrigue, not farmland.

claims.title: EP study: noise law not the cause
claims.claim: Study for the European Parliament's Committee on Petitions (Ecocentric Consulting, February 2026): Malta's noise problems are not caused by how it transposed and implements the Environmental Noise Directive, with only two meaningful non-conformity issues, because the noise people complain about (construction, entertainment, neighbourhood) falls outside the Directive's scope; it cites a 2019 survey in which 21% of Maltese ranked noise among their top four environmental issues against an EU28 average of 9%.
claims.counter: The conclusion follows from the study's evidence. The Directive sets only reporting thresholds (55 dB Lden and 50 dB Lnight, above the WHO 2018 levels of 53 and 45 dB for roads and 45 and 40 dB for aircraft) and excludes construction, entertainment and neighbourhood noise. Eurostat (ilc_mddw01), an all-source self-reported measure that includes road traffic (which the Directive covers) and so shows the size of the problem, not its cause, puts Malta first in the EU for reported street or neighbour noise, 31.3% against 18.1% in 2023, above the EU average in all 12 available years since 2010. Action-plan delays (plan due January 2025 unpublished at January 2026) are a genuine END implementation issue. Legal compliance is not the same as exposure below WHO levels. The transposition table and infringement record were not independently verified. The WHO levels and the EEA exposure figures are second-hand via the study (the study, citing EEA, says the END figures are likely a considerable underestimation). The 21% vs 9% figure is in ERA's consultation annex (pp. 5-6, in the Office of the Superintendent of Public Health's comment, no survey named; annex read via Wayback on 6 Oct 2026); it is not in the Marmarà October 2019 survey summary (mean worry score for noise 3.90 of 5 only), so its origin is unidentified.

claims.title: PM2.5 death rate down two-thirds
claims.claim: European Environment Agency (Air pollution quick country facts, 2025 country fact sheets): in Malta the rate of all-cause natural deaths attributable to long-term exposure to PM2.5 above 5 µg/m³, per 100 000 inhabitants aged 30 or over, is estimated to have fallen by 67.7% between 2005 and 2023 (from 143.5 to 46.3), resulting in 172 (95% CI 131-192) attributable deaths in 2023.
claims.counter: Every figure reproduces from the EEA's own burden-of-disease table and Eurostat sdg_11_52, which republishes it (143.5, 46.3, 67.74%, 172 (131-192)); the ETC HE technical report gives 173 (132-193), a one-death difference we cannot explain. From Eurostat natural deaths aged 30+ and the EEA's concentrations we get 346 (2005) and 170 (2023) deaths, within 1.2%. Measured PM2.5 fell: Msida -39% (2007-2023) and the three long-running stations -25% (2010-2023); this is direct evidence of a fall, not a check of the map, which is built on these stations. Caveats: no Maltese PM2.5 was reported to the EEA for 2005 (first valid day 29 August 2006), so the 2005 value (21.0 µg/m³) is a map value, from an older map method and model than 2023; the 95% CI covers the risk function only. PM10 at Msida and Żejtun did not fall while PM2.5 fell about 40%, and the PM2.5 instruments changed. The number of deaths fell 50.6% (348 to 172), as the population aged 30+ grew 54%; counting all concentrations the rate fell 54.7%, and from 2007 it fell 56.6%.
claims.speaker: European Environment Agency

subclaims.text: The rate was 143.5 per 100 000 aged 30+ in 2005
subclaims.finding: EEA table: 143.5 (348 deaths, 242,534 people aged 30+) [2]; Eurostat: 348 deaths [3].

subclaims.text: It was 46.3 in 2023
subclaims.finding: EEA table and technical report: 46.3 (35.2–51.7) [2, 6].

subclaims.text: “reduced by 67.7% between 2005 and 2023”
subclaims.finding: (143.5 − 46.3) / 143.5 = 67.74%. The 2005 value is a map value, from maps of another method and model, with no Maltese PM2.5 reported to the EEA [8, 10]; from 2007 the fall is 56.6%; the 95% CI covers the risk only [4].

subclaims.text: “172 (95% CI: 131-192) attributable deaths in 2023”
subclaims.finding: EEA table and Eurostat: 172 (131–192) [2, 3]. Technical report: 173 (132–193) [6]. The rate implies 172.8 deaths, but rounding does not explain the lower bound (35.2 → 131.4): a one-death difference, unexplained.

subclaims.text: Natural deaths, long-term exposure above 5 µg/m³, people aged 30+
subclaims.finding: Matches the documented method [4–6]; recomputed from Eurostat deaths within 1.2% (section 3).

claims.quote: In Malta, the rate of the all-cause natural deaths attributable to long-term exposure to fine particles (number of premature deaths attributable per 100 000 inhabitants 30 years or above) above 5µg/m3 is estimated to have been reduced by 67.7% between 2005 and 2023 (from 143.5 to 46.3, respectively), resulting in 172 (95% CI: 131-192) attributable deaths in 2023.

claims.title: 'Over 30% of our seas protected'
claims.claim: Environment Minister Miriam Dalli (2025, as quoted by Amphora Media): 'Malta protects more than 30% of its maritime zone'. ERA: the marine Natura 2000 network of 18 sites covers over 4,100 km2, 'more than 35% of Malta's Fisheries Management Zone'.
claims.counter: Mapped from EEA boundaries, Malta's 18 marine Natura 2000 sites cover 4,137.5 km2 of sea, and all of it lies within 25 nautical miles of the coast. That is 36.0% of the 25-nm Fisheries Management Zone (11,480 km2), which ERA names, but 7.8% of the EEZ as mapped internationally (52,923 km2) and 5.5% of the 75,715 km2 of sea Malta reports to the EU. Beyond 25 nm, about 64,000 km2 (85% of the waters reported to the EU) contains no marine protected site; even protecting the whole 25-nm zone would cover 15% of those waters. The deep sea (over 1,000 m, a quarter of the waters) is 0.6% protected. Reaching 30% on the EU basis needs ~18,600 km2 more. The minister's 'maritime zone' does not name the 25-nm zone.

claims.title: Commission: Malta to emit more in 2030 than in 2005
claims.claim: European Commission (EU Climate Action Progress Report 2025, COM(2025) 668, 6 Nov 2025): before any use of flexibilities, Malta's projected 2030 effort-sharing emissions leave a gap of 49 and 61 percentage points to its 19% reduction target, so Malta "is projected to emit more in 2030 than in 2005"; Malta is among the Member States with the largest projected gaps and (after banking, borrowing and the ETS flexibility) is projected to have excess emissions in 2026-2030. The Commission adds that, given the EU-wide surplus, it "cannot, at this stage, conclude" that Member States, taken together, are not making sufficient progress.
claims.counter: Reproduced. Malta's March 2025 projections (EEA) give 1,323.8 kt with planned measures and 1,450.1 kt with existing ones in 2030, against the legal 2005 level of 1,020.6 kt: +29.7% and +42.1%, gaps of 48.7 and 61.1 points to -19%. Above 2005 against every 2005 figure (EEA estimate 1,007.4 kt; 2013-2020 base year 1,116.1 kt: +18.6% at least) and with projections re-based on reviewed 2023 emissions (+26% / +38%). 2024 approximated emissions +40.8% (1,437 kt); over the yearly limit by 220, 257 and 301 kt in 2022-2024. Gap ranking with planned measures: Malta 48.7, Ireland 20.3, Germany 13.2 points (in tonnes Malta 0.5 Mt, Germany 64 Mt). Context and the other side: 2021-2030 balance -2.09 Mt (planned measures); the ETS flexibility (0.51 Mt) and the maximum land-use credit (0.03 Mt) leave 1.55 Mt to buy from other Member States (about 1% of the 125-175 Mt EU surplus) or cut; no safety reserve for Malta (Decision 2023/863). The Commission says it "cannot, at this stage, conclude" that Member States are not making sufficient progress. Malta's plan says the target rests on 2005 forecasts overtaken by population growth (the -19% was in fact set in 2018 on the basis of GDP per capita, with 2005 as the base year; population +41% to 2024; effort-sharing emissions per person flat at 2.53 t), and EU law (Regulation 2023/857) accepts the target is above Malta's cost-effective potential. "Missing its target" was the intake's paraphrase, not the Commission's wording.

But aircraft noise is mapped and published (round 3: 9,666 people at 55 dB Lden or more, 827 at 50 dB Lnight or more, 2016) and the Noise Action Plan states WHO health levels, and Freeport-area noise was measured in a Freeport-commissioned study (2014-15, second-hand via TVM) and a University of Malta study (2020-21: daytime averages 55 dBA or more at all five Birżebbuġa points; 98% of 477 respondents called noise a problem). No health-outcome study of residents near either site was found.
claims.speaker: ADPD - The Green Party

subclaims.text: Malta has yet to acknowledge the effect of Freeport noise on nearby residents' health
subclaims.finding: The Freeport is not mentioned in any ERA noise document and not among the mapped industrial sites, but a Freeport-commissioned study (2014–15 ◆) and a university study (2022) exist.

subclaims.text: Malta has yet to acknowledge the effect of airport noise on nearby residents' health
subclaims.finding: Aircraft noise exposure is modelled, mapped and published in three rounds, with WHO levels stated; no health assessment of residents.

subclaims.text: A study of the impact of noise from the Freeport and airport on nearby residents is needed
subclaims.finding: No health-outcome study found; local work is exposure, annoyance and self-reported symptoms.

claims.quote: This country has yet to acknowledge that noise pollution is having an effect on the health of those who live near the Freeport or the airport, including its points of access.

claims.title: Shearwaters: 10% of the world population
claims.claim: BirdLife Malta (LIFE Arċipelagu Garnija project page): Malta's Yelkouan shearwater population is estimated at around 1,600-1,800 pairs, about 10% of the global population.
claims.counter: ERA's Species Action Plan 2022-2030 gives 1,795-2,635 pairs (above the page's undated 1,600-1,800) and also says 'around 10%'. Global estimates: 11,355-54,524 pairs (Bourgeois & Vidal 2008, probably overestimated); 21,000-36,000 pairs (CIESM guide, second-hand). Malta's share is 4.4-8.6% (central 6.0%) with the page's own count and 5.0-12.5% (central 7.8%) with ERA's count. Tavolara (Sardinia) holds over half the world population (Pezzo et al. 2021).
claims.speaker: BirdLife Malta

subclaims.text: Malta’s population is around 1,600–1,800 pairs
subclaims.finding: Overlaps the regulator’s 1,795–2,635 pairs (2022–2030 plan); the page is undated and its count is the lower.

subclaims.text: …approximately 10% of the global population
subclaims.finding: 4.4–8.6% with the page’s own count; 5.0–12.5% with the regulator’s; central 6–8%. Global total poorly known.

claims.quote: Malta's population is estimated to be around 1,600 – 1,800 pairs, constituting approximately 10% of the global population.

claims.title: A net-zero Gozo by 2040
claims.claim: PN programme 2026: a clear and realistic plan for Gozo to become a Net-Zero Island by 2040, with afforestation among several measures. News summaries said net zero "through afforestation". (Checked as part of CC-011 until 5 Oct 2026.)
claims.counter: The programme promises a plan but publishes no baseline, boundary or pathway, and there is no official greenhouse-gas inventory for Gozo. A 2023 study for the EU islands secretariat put Gozo's energy-related CO2 at 118,000-154,000 t a year (2016-2020); our population-based estimate is about 157,000 t. Offsetting that by afforestation alone would need 4.9-6.3 times Gozo's land area at a measured semi-arid rate (1.5-8.5 times across a wider range). The PN's text relies on cuts first; "through afforestation" is a news summary.
claims.speaker: Nationalist Party

subclaims.text: A clear and realistic plan for a Net-Zero Gozo by 2040
subclaims.finding: No plan published; no official inventory or boundary. A 2023 energy baseline exists [6] but the programme does not use or cite it. Cannot be assessed as “realistic”.

subclaims.text: Gozo net zero through afforestation (news summary)
subclaims.finding: Would need 4.9–6.3 times Gozo’s area as new forest at a measured rate. Not the PN’s own wording.

subclaims.text: The first island in the Mediterranean where every unit of emissions is reduced or offset
subclaims.finding: Not tested.

pledge.target: A clear and realistic plan for Gozo to become a Net-Zero Island by 2040
pledge.vehicle: PN electoral programme 2026 (Nifs Ġdid), chapter Għawdex
pledge.note: No baseline, boundary or pathway published and no greenhouse-gas inventory for Gozo. The PN lost the 30 May 2026 election, so this is an opposition proposal.

claims.quote: Infasslu pjan ċar u realistiku biex sal-2040, Għawdex isir Net-Zero Island

claims.title: WSC: a net-zero impact on groundwater
claims.claim: The Water Services Corporation says its Net Zero Impact Utility project (EU co-financed) will give back to the environment at least as much natural freshwater as it abstracts, minimising its impact on the water environment. Government proposals on groundwater abstraction (reported as the Energy and Water Agency's Green Paper, 2023) exempt WSC's boreholes from new groundwater tariffs because WSC is said to be moving towards a net-zero impact on the groundwater environment, with its abstraction capped at 14 million m3 a year to 2030.
claims.counter: Not yet checked. Context from CC-009: WSC's groundwater production fell to about 11.5 million m3 in 2025 while national fresh groundwater abstraction was about 38.5 million m3 in 2024 (Eurostat, estimates), mostly by agriculture; Malta's 3rd-cycle EU reporting lists 4 of 15 groundwater bodies in poor quantitative status and all 15 in poor chemical status. A net-zero impact claim needs a defined balance (what is "given back", where, and how it is measured), not only lower WSC abstraction.
claims.speaker: Water Services Corporation; Energy and Water Agency

claims.title: EU: transport is 48% of effort-sharing emissions
claims.claim: European Commission (2026 Country Report - Malta, 3 Jun 2026): "Transport is the dominant source of Malta's effort sharing emissions. It has generated 48% of these emissions in 2024, up by 45% since 2005."
claims.counter: On the effort-sharing definition (all domestic transport, aviation CO2 excluded; the definition of the report's own Graph 3.1) transport was 53.3% of Malta's effort-sharing emissions in 2024 in the EEA approximated inventory and in the report's Graph 3.1, and 53% in the Commission's CAPR 2025 Malta profile; 54.8% on the final 2026 inventory (our estimate of the total). Only road transport alone over an ESR total gives 48% (47.5-48.3%; our identification; the report does not say how 48% was computed). The 45% reproduces exactly as the rise in transport emissions (+45.0% on approximated 2024 data, 0.528 to 0.766 Mt; +48.4% on the final inventory); the share barely moved (52.0% to 53.3%). Footnote (140) and Table A8.1 call the sector "road transport", but the table's series includes domestic shipping (11.9% of it in 2024, +184% since 2005). 2024 values are approximated; final data after the 2027 review.
claims.speaker: European Commission

subclaims.text: Transport is the dominant source of Malta’s effort sharing emissions
subclaims.finding: 53.3% in 2024 on the approximated data; the next sector, small industry, 19%. The largest sector in every year 2005–2024 [5, 6].

subclaims.text: It has generated 48% of these emissions in 2024
subclaims.finding: 53% on the report’s own definition: EEA approximated inventory and Graph 3.1 53.3%, Commission climate profile 53% [1, 5, 8]. Only road-transport-only ratios (47.5–48.3%) give 48% (our identification).

subclaims.text: … up by 45% since 2005
subclaims.finding: The rise in emissions, not in the share: +45.0% on approximated 2024 data (0.528 to 0.766 Mt); +48.4% on the final 2026 inventory [1, 5, 6]. The share moved from 52.0% to 53.3%.

subclaims.text: Effort sharing covers “road transport”; Table A8.1 row “domestic road transport”
subclaims.finding: Effort sharing covers all domestic transport except aviation CO2 [2, 3]. The table row matches that wider series to 0.1 points in 2018–2023 and exactly in 2024 (45.0%); road alone is up to 6.2 points off (2024: +39.4%). Shipping is 11.9% of it [6].

claims.quote: Transport is the dominant source of Malta’s effort sharing emissions. It has generated 48% of these emissions in 2024 (141), up by 45% since 2005.

claims.title: EU: 37.7% of new cars zero-emission
claims.claim: European Commission (2026 Country Report - Malta, 3 Jun 2026): in 2024 Malta recorded 7,700 new passenger car registrations, of which 37.7% were zero-emission vehicles, well above the EU average of 13.6%.
claims.counter: Eurostat: 7,683 new cars in 2024, 2,893 battery electric, no hydrogen: 37.65% (2023: 20.31%; 2025: 37.56%). EU-27 13.53% (report 13.6%). Malta is 2nd of 27 after Denmark (51.3%). Context: zero-emission cars were 2.2% of the passenger-car stock at the end of 2024 (EU 2.2%) and the stock grew by 6,632 cars (18 a day); the report notes charging infrastructure lags.
claims.speaker: European Commission

subclaims.text: 7 700 new passenger cars in 2024, 37.7% of them zero-emission
subclaims.finding: Eurostat: 7,683 new cars, 2,893 battery electric, no hydrogen: 37.65%.

subclaims.text: Up 17.4 points from 20.3% in 2023
subclaims.finding: 2023 share 20.31%. The rise is 17.34 points from unrounded shares, 17.35 from the report’s own annex values.

subclaims.text: Well above the EU average of 13.6%
subclaims.finding: Eurostat EU-27: 13.53%. Malta is second of 27 member states, after Denmark.

claims.quote: In 2024, Malta recorded 7 700 new passenger car registrations, of which 37.7% were ZEVs - a 17.4 percentage point increase since 2023 (20.3%) and well above the EU average of 13.6%.

claims.title: EU: 621 kg of waste a head, 74% landfilled
claims.claim: European Commission (2026 Country Report - Malta, 3 Jun 2026): Malta generated 621 kg of waste per person in 2024 against an EU average of 517 kg, and its landfill rate fell from 82% to 74% over ten years but remains well above the EU average of 22% (2023).
claims.counter: All figures reproduce from Eurostat env_wasmun: 621 kg (EU 517 kg, provisional) in 2024; landfilled as a share of waste generated 82.0% in 2013 and 73.6% in 2023 (72.1% in 2024); incineration 2.7% in 2023. Malta is 3rd-highest for the landfill rate in 2023 (after Greece and Romania) and highest of 20 states with 2024 data; 6th-highest for waste per person in 2024. EU-27 2023 landfill rate not published (22.6% in 2022, 21.3% in 2024). The fall from 82% to 74% came mostly in 2023 (83.3% in 2022). The Shift's 79.2% (CC-081) is the 2024 share of waste treated, a different denominator.
claims.speaker: European Commission

subclaims.text: 621 kg of waste per person in 2024, against an EU average of 517 kg
subclaims.finding: Eurostat env_wasmun: Malta 621 kg, EU-27 517 kg (provisional). Malta is sixth-highest of 20 states with 2024 data.

subclaims.text: Landfill rate down from 82% to 74% over ten years
subclaims.finding: 82.0% (2013) and 73.6% (2023), landfilled as a share of generated. Most of the fall came in 2023.

subclaims.text: Still one of the highest in the EU, well above the EU average of 22% (2023)
subclaims.finding: Third-highest in 2023 (after Greece and Romania); highest of 20 states in 2024. EU-27 2023 not published; 22.6% in 2022 and 21.3% in 2024.

claims.quote: Waste generation is still high with 621 kg per person generated in 2024 (compared with the EU average of 517 kg per person) … Over the last 10 years, Malta has brought its landfill rate down from 82% to 74%. However, this is still one of the highest in the EU, and well above the EU average of 22% (2023).

claims.title: IMF: population up 25% in a decade
claims.claim: International Monetary Fund staff (Selected Issues, Feb 2026): Malta's population rose by 25 percent over a decade, largely due to immigration.
claims.counter: Eurostat demo_gind: growth was 24.4-24.6% over the decades ending 1 Jan 2020, 2021 and 2022, but 30.9% over 1 Jan 2015-2025 (the latest decade available in Feb 2026) and 30.8% over 2016-2026. The paper gives no years. Net migration was 93-97% of growth in every decade since 2010-2020. EU-27 grew 1.9% over 2015-2025.
claims.speaker: International Monetary Fund

subclaims.text: Malta’s population rose by 25 percent over a decade
subclaims.finding: 24.4–24.6% for the decades ending 2020–2022; 30.9% for 2015–2025, the latest decade available in Feb 2026. No years given.

subclaims.text: …largely due to immigration
subclaims.finding: Net migration was 93–97% of the growth in every decade since 2010–2020; natural change was small.

claims.quote: Malta’s population rose by 25 percent over a decade, largely due to immigration.

claims.title: EEA: Malta among highest fossil-fuel subsidies
claims.claim: European Environment Agency (indicator page, 29 Jan 2025): in 2023 fossil-fuel subsidies represented the highest shares of GDP in Malta, Poland and Slovakia, all at or above 1.5%.
claims.counter: The IMF's 2025 Article IV report estimates Malta's energy subsidy cost falling from about 1.8% of GDP in 2022 to about 0.8% in 2025 (see CC-022); the Government plans about EUR 400 million of energy support to 2027 (CC-095). The EEA's definition of a fossil-fuel subsidy (including support that lowers consumer prices) differs from budget lines.
claims.speaker: European Environment Agency
claims.quote: In 2023, fossil fuel subsidies represented the highest shares of gross domestic product (GDP) in Malta, Poland, and Slovakia (all at or above 1.5%).

claims.title: PN: only EU state with rising emissions intensity
claims.claim: Nationalist Party MP Eve Borg Bonello (26 Jan 2026): Malta is the only EU Member State that, instead of reducing, has increased the intensity of its greenhouse-gas emissions since 2013; it rose 17% while the EU average fell 34%.
claims.counter: The Government says per-capita emissions fell over 44% and emissions per unit of GDP over 80% since 2005 (CC-025, CC-003): the base year (2005 versus 2013) and the metric differ. Economic output grew fast, so intensity can rise even when the level is flat; the reverse also applies.
claims.speaker: Nationalist Party (PN)
claims.quote: Malta is the only EU Member State that, instead of reducing, has increased the intensity of its greenhouse gas emissions since 2013.

claims.title: Chamber: congestion cost EUR 770m, 3.4% of GDP
claims.claim: The Malta Chamber of Commerce, Enterprise and Industry (LEAD proposals for the 2026-2031 legislature, 14 May 2026): traffic congestion cost the economy an estimated EUR 770 million in 2025, equivalent to 3.4% of GDP.
claims.counter: The EUR 770m is quoted accurately from the National Transport Master Plan 2030 (p. 124), which projects EUR 917m by 2030 and excludes EUR 195.4m of environmental costs, but the plan publishes no derivation for 2025 (its appraisal annex models 2030 and 2060 only). EUR 770m is 3.12% of 2025 GDP at current prices (Eurostat EUR 24,664m); 3.34% of 2024 GDP; 3.8-3.9% of real GDP. 3.4% would need GDP of EUR 22.6bn. Marco Cremona's EUR 1.13bn estimate (MNA, 3 Jun 2026) is second-hand.
claims.speaker: The Malta Chamber of Commerce, Enterprise and Industry

subclaims.text: Traffic congestion cost the economy an estimated €770 million in 2025
subclaims.finding: Accurately cited from the National Transport Master Plan 2030, p. 124. The plan publishes no derivation for 2025, so the figure cannot be tested.

subclaims.text: …equivalent to 3.4% of GDP
subclaims.finding: 3.12% of 2025 GDP at current prices; 3.34% of 2024 GDP; 3.8–3.9% of real GDP. No published series gives 3.4%.

claims.quote: In 2025, traffic congestion imposed an estimated cost of €770 million on the Maltese economy, equivalent to 3.4% of GDP.

claims.title: UNESCO: Valletta setting not safeguarded
claims.claim: UNESCO World Heritage Committee (2025 state-of-conservation decision, as reported): Malta's current planning policies and regulations do not sufficiently safeguard Valletta's setting; the Committee asked for effective height controls within and around the property, a further-developed buffer zone, and an updated conservation report by 1 December 2026.
claims.counter: The Government treated the later deadline as a sign of confidence in its heritage management and rejected the Opposition's 'alarmism' (Lovin Malta, reported); the PN asked for a local-plan revision (MaltaToday). The Planning Authority's Floor Area Ratio policy and height rules are the policies at issue.

location.place: City of Valletta World Heritage Site

claims.speaker: UNESCO World Heritage Committee

themes.name: Sealed soil and concrete
themes.description: Excavation, concrete and sealed surfaces around trees. The EU review notes sealed or degraded soil keeps increasing in Malta.

themes.name: Replanting as currency
themes.description: Tree losses are justified by promised replacement or transplanting. Test survival and net canopy, not planting counts.

themes.name: Water chain: farm waste, sewage, sea, aquifer
themes.description: The Commission blames farm waste in the sewers for poor treatment; agricultural nitrates are behind groundwater failure. Treated water also feeds 'new water' irrigation.

themes.name: Transport, air and climate
themes.description: Fleet growth links traffic claims, air quality and emissions. The climate report names transport and buildings as the lagging sectors.

themes.name: Waste and construction
themes.description: Inert mineral waste dominates Malta's recycling statistics, which ties waste claims to development projects. ERA and NSO confirm construction waste was about 2.2 of 2.9 Mt generated in 2023; the link to specific projects is still indicative.

themes.name: Selective-metric pattern
themes.description: A favourable metric is cited while the regulator-relevant metric looks worse. Useful for tagging, not for implying a common cause.

themes.name: 2030 carbon target
themes.description: The Climate Action Authority and the 2026 Labour manifesto (priority 18) both state a 40% cut in carbon emissions by 2030 against 2005, without saying whether it covers total or effort-sharing emissions.

themes.name: Planning, housing and land take
themes.description: Permit volumes, enforcement and housing demand drive land take. Claims about prices, enforcement, reclamation and land loss rest on the same planning system and the same data (PA permits, NSO prices, land-cover maps).

themes.name: Compliance-not-health pattern
themes.description: Meeting an EU legal limit or procedure is presented as if it meant a health-protective level: air (WHO PM2.5 guideline) and noise (WHO noise guidelines).

themes.name: Tourism pressure and carrying capacity
themes.description: Record arrivals, hotel pipelines and concessions on public land: claims about tourism growth and its limits share one driver. Indicative until a report tests it.

themes.name: Heat, power cuts and health
themes.description: The July heatwaves, the power cuts that accompanied them, and the health response: claims about causes (heat vs generation), deaths, worker exposure and disclosure share one event and one data gap (where deaths occurred, and whether outages coincided).

themes.name: Oversight and disclosure
themes.description: How public bodies respond to scrutiny: an Ombudsman finding left unimplemented, and a request for data refused with a promise to publish later. Useful for tracking follow-through; not evidence of a common cause.

themes.name: Noise governance
themes.description: Claims about whether Malta maps, plans for and acts on noise under Directive 2002/49/EC and the WHO guidelines: the 2026 EP study, the PN petition and ADPD's call for a Freeport and airport study.

themes.name: Energy subsidies
themes.description: Claims about what energy support costs and what it shields: the lowest-electricity-burden claim, the EUR 400 million to 2027, and the EEA ranking of fossil-fuel subsidies by share of GDP. They rest on different definitions of subsidy; indicative until a report tests them together.

themes.name: Heritage and development control
themes.description: Permits and planning policy near protected heritage: the Ġgantija buffer zone, Fort Chambray and UNESCO's request for height controls around Valletta. Indicative until a report tests the permits and policies.

pledge_labels.name: Not measurable
pledge_labels.meaning: the pledge as worded has no definition, baseline or date against which delivery could be checked.

pledge_labels.name: Not yet due
pledge_labels.meaning: the pledge is measurable, its deadline or term has not passed, and no progress data have been published yet.

pledge_labels.name: On track
pledge_labels.meaning: published progress is at or ahead of a straight-line path (or the pledge's own milestones) to the target by the deadline.

pledge_labels.name: Off track
pledge_labels.meaning: published progress is behind that path, and the target has not yet been shown to be met or missed.

pledge_labels.name: Met
pledge_labels.meaning: documents or data show the target was reached, by the deadline if one was set.

pledge_labels.name: Missed
pledge_labels.meaning: the deadline or term has passed, and documents or data that can be shown say the target was not reached.
